newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: FEATURE-Sri Lankan elephants battle for survival.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Sri Lankan elephants battle for survival.

text.p: Papaya, crumpled banana leaves and smashed furniture litter the trail of destruction the elephant has left across the compound.
It came after nightfall when the family was at the temple, so no one was killed. But the damage was still overwhelming.
With its broken coconut-thatch roof lying lopsided, the house is now just a heap of sticks, leaving the family little shelter from the sun and the monsoon rains.

"We heard warning fire-crackers being lit and knew that an elephant had come. We ran back but it was a big one and when we shouted, it chased us and then brought our house down and four or five trees," said Davage Seelin, surveying the wreckage.
Seelin's story is typical. Her family was homeless before the government gave her 3.5 acres (1.4 hectares) of jungle to clear for a house and grow rice and cashew nuts.
But when the farmers of Puriyakulama cut down and burnt the forest and scrub for paddy fields, the wildlife was forgotten.
DISAPPEARING JUNGLE

In the past 70 years, more than 60 percent of the Indian Ocean island's jungle has been turned into farmland. Much of the remaining forest is in national parks and these relatively small enclaves are separated by large swathes of agricultural land.
Now Puriyakulama, close to an important water hole, is the site of a war of attrition between Sri Lanka's biggest animal and the island's expanding rural population.
Pushed back into ever smaller pockets of jungle and with limited access to their traditional roaming areas, elephants are coming into daily conflict with farmers and smallholders.
They are fighting a losing battle for survival.

Officials and conservationists say Sri Lanka's elephant population is falling at an alarming rate. The country now has only 2,500 to 3,000 wild elephants, down from an estimated 12,000 at the turn of the century.
"If things continue as they are, the situation looks very bleak for the elephant," said Mangala de Silva, a professor of zoology working for the government's wildlife service.
Before independence in 1948, many elephant deaths were the result of hunting as British colonial rulers shot for sport and local traders and poachers killed males for their ivory tusks.
FARMERS PROTECT THEMSELVES
But these days most elephants are shot or poisoned by farmers protecting themselves, their homes and their crops.
The director of Sri Lanka's Wildlife Conservation service, N.W. Dissanayake, says 110 elephants died in 1995 and 100 or so in 1996. This year at least 50 have been killed.

The villagers are right to be worried by elephants. The number of people killed in attacks has risen sharply, with at least 59 deaths reported in 1996, up from 29 in 1993. Over 250 people have been killed by elephants in the past five years.
And the damage to farms is enormous.
"Elephants find cultivated land easy pickings," said Jayanthe Jayewardene, a conservationist and author of a popular book on Sri Lankan elephants.
"A four-tonne elephant can destroy six months' work on the farm in one night. If it is allowed to eat, it can consume up to 200 kg (440 lb) of paddy before daybreak," he said.
But experts say the elephants cannot be blamed.
NO CHOICE FOR ELEPHANTS
"Now elephants don't have sufficient habitat, not enough food, not enough water. They have no choice but to enter into cultivation," said Dissanayake.
Five miles (eight km) away from Puriyakulama in the village of Karuwalagaswewa, ranger Waniarachchi Jayaweera inspects a heap of broken red baked-mud bricks in a patch of cleared bush.
"Elephant has been through here because it is on their path to the irrigation tank. There is jungle on both sides of the road and this house was on their crossing point," he said.

The village has special problems with elephants because of its location. In the northwest of the island, it is close to an area of jungle frequented by rebels of the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE).
The LTTE are fighting a 14-year-old war with the Sri Lankan government for a separate homeland for the minority Tamil population in the island's north and east.
Soldiers patrolling the village say elephants are driven out of the forest periodically by the movement of the guerrillas and by the sound of gunfire and explosions.
Jayewardene says the ethnic conflict has made protection of elephants' natural habitat more difficult since many of the animals live in areas where the conflict has been intense.
"The LTTE have sometimes shot at elephants because they drink up the water supply. There have also been reports of elephants having their legs blown off by landmines," he said.
Squeezed between the rebels on one side and subsistence farmers on the other, elephant numbers are dwindling.
"If the problem is not addressed, there is a risk that in 30 to 40 years, the elephant population will be reduced to a level where it can no longer reproduce itself," Jayewardene said.
FATE NOT YET SEALED
But Jayewardene says the fate of Sri Lanka's wild elephants is not yet sealed if the right steps are taken.
"Is there a future for the elephant? Yes. Given a habitat and proper management," he said.
Dissanayake agrees. He wants to stop the opening of forest cover and to designate corridors of vegetation between some of the country's existing national parks and sanctuaries.

His department is building trenches and electric fences around parks to try to keep elephant herds away from people, renovating water holes and employing a network of veterinary surgeons to help elephants if they are injured.
"I don't think we have to be pessimistic," said Dissanayake. "Elephant today is our special beast here in Sri Lanka and it will remain so, I think forever, because people love elephants."
Back in Puriyakulama, Seelin is not so enthusiastic.
"It will be very difficult to build a new home," she said. "I don't know if we could rebuild it even in six months."
